etymology.text: Originally a pictogram of a trident-like weapon or tool; borrowed for its sound to write the pronoun ‘I’ already in the oracle-bone script. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ŋa.

funFacts: The character 我 was first a drawing of a weapon with a toothed blade; it only stands for ‘I’ because the words sounded alike.
pitfalls: 我 is both ‘I’ and ‘me’ — no case change: 他喜欢我 ‘he likes me’.
‘My’ is 我的 + noun (我的菜); 的 is dropped only before relatives and close relations (我妈妈, 我朋友).
Third-tone sandhi: 我很好 wǒ hěn hǎo is spoken wó hén hǎo (written tones stay).
subtleties: Chinese leaves out 我 when it is obvious: asked 你喜欢吗？ you can answer just 喜欢。
In formal writing 我 can mean ‘our’: 我国 (our country), 我校 (our school).

etymology.text: Pictogram of a snake (the snake is now written 蛇); the character was borrowed for the then-homophonous third-person pronoun. Today 他 is written for ‘he’, 她 for ‘she’ and 它 for things and animals.

funFacts: Spoken Chinese has one third-person pronoun, tā. 他, 她 and 它 are distinctions of writing only — introduced in the early 20th century.
它 began as a drawing of a snake; the snake later got its own character 蛇, with the insect radical 虫.
pitfalls: There is no ‘dummy it’: ‘It is me’ is 是我, ‘It is raining’ is 下雨了 — no 它.
For things Chinese uses 它 much less than English uses ‘it’: asked where the phone is, people answer 在这儿 ‘(it is) here’, without 它.
subtleties: Many people write 他 or 她 for their own pet, to show affection.
In writing 它 also refers to abstract things: 这个问题很重要，我们要解决它 ‘this problem is important, we must solve it’.

etymology.text: Origin unclear. In Classical Chinese 是 was a pronoun ‘this’; the development ‘this > be right, correct > to be’ gave the copula, which emerged by the Eastern Han dynasty.

funFacts: In Classical Chinese 是 meant ‘this’ — the modern ‘is’ grew out of the pronoun.
pitfalls: No 是 before adjectives: 西红柿很红 (the tomato is red), not *西红柿是红.
The negation is always 不是 (bú shì), never *没是.
As ‘yes’, 是 fits questions with 是 or confirms a statement; to 你要吗？ answer 要。, to 你有吗？ answer 有。
subtleties: 是 can also say what fills a place: 桌子上都是书 ‘the table is covered with books’.
是的 is a softer, very common ‘yes’; a bare 是 can sound like ‘Yes, sir’.
To agree with what someone just said, 对 (duì, ‘right, correct’) is the most common ‘yes’: 你是老师？— 对。

Other readings: hè (附和 ‘to echo’), huó (和面 ‘to knead dough’), hú (winning at mahjong).

For ‘with (a person)’ 和 and 跟 are interchangeable before 一起: 我和 / 跟朋友一起吃饭; 跟 is more colloquial (S11).

funFacts: The progressive use (他在吃饭 ‘he is eating’) grew out of the place meaning — literally ‘he is at eating’.
pitfalls: Known thing + 在 + place: 西红柿在这里 ‘the tomatoes are here’. Place + 有 + new thing: 这里有西红柿 ‘there are tomatoes here’.
Negate with 不: 他不在 ‘he isn’t in’.
Progressive 在 vs place 在: 他在吃饭 ‘he is eating’, 他在家吃饭 ‘he eats at home’ (or ‘is eating at home’) — the place version has a place after 在.
subtleties: 在 + place goes before the verb: 我在家吃饭, not *我吃饭在家.
The progressive can be strengthened with 正 and 呢: 他正在吃饭呢 ‘he’s eating right now’; its negation is 没(在): 他没在吃饭.

etymology.text: 孩 ‘child’ (semantic 子 + phonetic 亥) + the toneless noun suffix 子.

funFacts: The toneless suffix 子 makes nouns: 孩子, and in the home lesson 桌子, 椅子, 杯子, 盘子.
pitfalls: 孩子 is both ‘a child (young)’ and ‘someone’s child’: 我的孩子 can be forty years old.
A child is never 小人 — 小人 means a petty, mean person.
subtleties: 孩子们 is the children as a group, but not after a number: 三个孩子.

readings.none: one reading for all its senses

tradPerSense.none: written the same in traditional characters

toneSandhi.none: no 一 or 不 in the word

profile.feeling: The most basic word for a human being — singular or plural as the context needs.

senses.def: people (a bare 人 is singular or plural: 很多人 ‘many people’)
a person of some place or kind: 希腊人 ‘a Greek’, 工人 ‘worker’

examples.tr: There are lots of people here.
There are three people at the door.
Don’t mind what other people say.

phrases.tr: mountains of people, seas of people
people cannot be judged by their looks
phrases.meaning: don’t judge a book by its cover (full: 人不可貌相，海水不可斗量)

synonyms.nuance: ‘people’ in general statements (人们常说… ‘people often say…’); never after a number or measure word
‘mankind, humanity’ — science, philosophy
‘personage, people (of a circle)’ — 各界人士 ‘people from all walks of life’
‘guy, fellow’ — familiar, can be rude

etymology.text: Pictogram: the side view of a standing person, with an arm and a leg.

funFacts: As a component 人 often becomes 亻 on the left of a character: 你, 他, 们 and 位 all contain it.
pitfalls: Counted with a measure word: 三个人 — but members of a household are counted with 口: 我家有四口人.
‘People’ is usually just 人 (很多人); 人们 never takes a number: *三个人们.
subtleties: Nationalities are country + 人: 希腊人 (Greek), 德国人 (German), 中国人 (Chinese).
人 is the second syllable of 男人 and 女人, but each of those is a word of its own.

readings.none: one reading for all its senses

tradPerSense.none: written the same in traditional characters

toneSandhi.none: no 一 or 不 in the word

profile.feeling: Warmth and trust; friendship (关系) matters a lot in Chinese social life.

senses.def: boyfriend / girlfriend (in 男朋友, 女朋友)
in 小朋友: a friendly word for a child

examples.py: Xiǎo péngyou, nǐ jǐ suì le?
examples.tr: How old are you, little one?

phrases.text: 有朋自远方来，不亦乐乎？
phrases.tr: Is it not a joy to have friends come from afar?
phrases.meaning: a classic line to welcome friends or guests from far away
fair-weather friends, friends only for the good times

synonyms.nuance: ‘good friend’ — written; also a ‘friend’ on social media
‘buddy, mate’ between men
a woman’s best (female) friend
‘partner, companion’ — in play, work or business

etymology.text: 朋 (originally two strings of cowrie shells — a pair, companions) + 友 (two hands — friendship); the second syllable is toneless.

funFacts: Like German ‘mein Freund’, 男朋友 ‘male friend’ means ‘boyfriend’ — say 我的一个朋友 ‘a friend of mine’ to avoid the romantic sense.
Adults call children 小朋友 ‘little friend’.
pitfalls: The second syllable is toneless: péngyou.
我朋友 and 我的朋友 are both fine ‘my friend’; but 女朋友 means ‘girlfriend’, not ‘female friend’.
subtleties: In speeches and online, 朋友们 ‘friends!’ addresses an audience warmly.

readings.none: one reading for all its senses

tradPerSense.none: traditional 學生 for every sense

toneSandhi.none: no 一 or 不 in the word

override.measure: Wiktionary lists only 位 for 學生; 个 is the everyday measure word (一个学生) and 名 the formal one (两名学生) in every Mandarin dictionary.

profile.feeling: School bags and exams — the everyday word for anyone who studies.

examples.py: Wǒmen bān yǒu sānshí ge xuésheng.
examples.tr: There are thirty students in our class.

examples.py: Tā shì Běijīng Dàxué de xuésheng.
examples.tr: He is a student at Peking University.

examples.py: Tā shì Qí Báishí de xuésheng.
examples.tr: He was a disciple of (the painter) Qi Baishi.

synonyms.nuance: ‘classmate’ — also how students and teachers address a student (这位同学…)
‘trainee’ — in a course, a driving school, a training programme
male / female students — the everyday school words
‘scholars, students’ — speeches and headlines

etymology.text: 学 ‘to learn’ + 生 ‘one who …’ (生 ‘to grow, to live’, a sprout coming out of the ground).

funFacts: A teacher calls on a pupil with 这位同学 ‘this classmate’ — 同学 is used as a polite address for students.
pitfalls: Standard Beijing speech makes the second syllable light: xuésheng; xuéshēng is also heard.
Count with a measure word: 三个学生, or formally 三名学生 — never *三学生.
subtleties: 名 is the measure word of official counts (news, forms): 两名学生 ‘two students’.

readings.none: one reading for all its senses

tradPerSense.none: traditional 老師 for every sense

toneSandhi.none: no 一 or 不 in the word

profile.feeling: Respect: the teacher holds an honoured place in Chinese culture.

senses.def: a title and form of address for a teacher (王老师 ‘Teacher Wang’)
a polite address for a respected expert, writer or artist

examples.text: 我们的中文老师是北京人。
examples.py: Wǒmen de Zhōngwén lǎoshī shì Běijīngrén.
examples.tr: Our Chinese teacher is from Beijing.
Good morning, teacher! (a class greeting its teacher)

phrases.tr: teacher for one day, father for life
phrases.meaning: you owe your teacher lifelong respect

synonyms.nuance: the profession — 教师节 ‘Teachers’ Day’; not used as an address
academic supervisor, mentor
‘master’ — for craftsmen, drivers, cooks; also a polite address for workers
‘teacher, master’ in older usage; today mostly ‘Mr’

etymology.text: 老 (a prefix of respect and familiarity, from ‘old’) + 师 ‘teacher, master’.

funFacts: Teachers’ Day is 10 September in mainland China; Taiwan celebrates it on 28 September, Confucius’ traditional birthday.
pitfalls: 老师 is a title placed after the surname: 王老师 — not *老师王; address your teacher as 老师, not by first name.
老 here does not mean ‘old’: a 25-year-old teacher is still 老师.
subtleties: In mainland China 老师 has spread as a polite address for writers, artists and other experts.
Measure word: 一位老师 (polite) or 一个老师; 位 is never used for yourself: 我是老师, not *我是一位老师.

profile.feeling: The first number — and, with a measure word, the Chinese way to say ‘a, an’.

senses.def: a, an — one (with a measure word: 一本书 ‘a book’)
whole, all (一屋子人 ‘a whole room full of people’)

examples.text: 我一到家就给你打电话。
examples.py: Wǒ yí dào jiā jiù gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.
examples.tr: As soon as I get home I’ll call you.

phrases.meaning: to kill two birds with one stone

synonyms.nuance: yāo: ‘one’ when reading out phone and room numbers, so it is not confused with 七 qī (110 = yāo yāo líng)

etymology.text: Ideogram: a single horizontal stroke for the number one. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ʔit.

funFacts: When reading phone or room numbers aloud, Chinese say yāo instead of yī for 1, so it cannot be misheard as 七 qī.
pitfalls: Tone changes: yí before a 4th tone (一个 yí ge, 一下 yí xià), yì before the other tones (一本 yì běn, 一张 yì zhāng), but yī when counting, in numbers and at the end (第一 dì-yī, 十一 shíyī).
Between 一 and the noun there must be a measure word: 一本书, never *一书.
subtleties: Chinese needs 一 + measure word much less often than English needs ‘a’: 这是书 ‘this is a book’ is fine.
一 + measure word introduces one new thing; a thing already known goes bare before the verb: 书在这里 ‘the book is here’.

readings.none: one reading for all its senses

tradPerSense.none: written the same in traditional characters

features.toneSandhi: yí before a 4th tone (一个 yí ge), yì before the 1st–3rd tones (一本 yì běn); yī alone, in counting, in dates and ordinals

absent.reason: Chinese has no definite article. A thing already known is a bare noun, usually placed before the verb: 书在这里 ‘the book is here’, 钥匙不在这里 ‘the keys aren’t here’. When pointing is needed, 这 / 那 + measure word does it: 这本书 ‘this book’.
absent.use: a bare noun before the verb; 这 / 那 + measure word when it must be explicit
